title: Booking walkthrough · Three messages, one appointment
subtitle: Follow one example Telegram conversation from the first webhook to the committed booking and final reply.

transcript.speaker: CAPY
transcript.text:
Here are the available times. Choose a time below or reply with its number:
1. 2026-10-20 15:00 UTC with Alex
2. 2026-10-20 17:00 UTC with Alex

transcript.speaker: CAPY
transcript.text: Please confirm Massage with Alex on October 20, 2026 at 15:00 (UTC). Reply “yes” to book or “no” to leave it unbooked.

transcript.speaker: CAPY
transcript.text: Booked: Massage with Alex on October 20, 2026 at 15:00 (UTC).

transcriptContext: Synthetic example from the golden booking fixture. Today is October 19, 2026 in the studio’s UTC timezone.

lanes.label: Turn 1 · Customer asks for a massage tomorrow

nodes.title: “Book Massage tomorrow.”
nodes.detail: Telegram POSTs a private message to the authenticated webhook.
nodes.why: Authenticating the bot at the webhook gives the turn a trusted business identity before CAPY uses the message.

nodes.title: Accept update
nodes.detail: Save the update and schedule a wake-up before returning HTTP 204.
nodes.why: The database commit gives Telegram a safe acknowledgment boundary. If the webhook fails earlier, Telegram can retry without creating a second inbox row.

nodes.title: Wake the worker
nodes.detail: The relay publishes bot and chat IDs for the incoming queue.
nodes.why: An ID-only wake-up keeps the customer message in PostgreSQL and lets the relay retry publication independently.

nodes.title: Claim the chat head
nodes.detail: Lease this update. The worker resolves the sender and invokes LangGraph.
nodes.why: A chat lease prevents competing workers from applying messages to different versions of the same draft.

nodes.title: Extract service and date
nodes.detail: Gemma resolves Massage on October 20, 2026 from the sanitized message.
nodes.why: Separating fact extraction from routing lets a later step make a decision from explicit service and date values.

lanes.label: Turn 1 · Find and send two numbered times

nodes.title: Send the two choices
nodes.detail: CAPY offers 15:00 and 17:00 UTC with Alex. The business still has no new booking.
nodes.why: Numbered choices let the customer select a concrete appointment with a short reply that CAPY can resolve later.

nodes.title: Reserve and deliver reply
nodes.detail: A sender wake-up contains an outbox ID. The sender reserves the reply.
nodes.why: Reserving before sending lets multiple sender processes share Telegram rate limits and preserve reply order for the chat.

nodes.title: Save offer and queue reply
nodes.detail: Publish the Redis checkpoint pointer and queue the reply in PostgreSQL.
nodes.why: Committing the checkpoint pointer and reply together makes the stored offers available as soon as the customer can see them.

nodes.title: Find available slots
nodes.detail: Search for fits. LangGraph saves the numbered offer list in Redis.
nodes.why: Availability comes from business hours and current bookings, so the options reflect the actual calendar.

nodes.title: Choose availability search
nodes.detail: Laya proposes a search. Python checks service and date.
nodes.why: A model proposal can guide the conversation while Python checks that the catalog and date support a search.

lanes.label: Turn 2 · Customer chooses the first time

nodes.detail: Telegram sends a new update for the same chat.
nodes.why: A separate update preserves the sequence from the offered list to the selected appointment.

nodes.title: Save the selection update
nodes.detail: Record this update under its own Telegram update ID.
nodes.why: A stable update ID lets the inbox recognize a redelivery of the same choice.

nodes.title: Wake the same chat
nodes.detail: Send the same bot and chat IDs to the incoming queue.
nodes.why: The worker uses these IDs to find the chat's next eligible message.

nodes.title: Claim the selection
nodes.detail: Lease the new head and read the published checkpoint reference.
nodes.why: The worker must use the draft published by the last completed turn for the number to keep its original meaning.

nodes.title: Restore the previous offer
nodes.detail: Copy the completed Redis state into the selection attempt.
nodes.why: A fresh attempt thread keeps partial work separate from the last successful copy of the offered times.

lanes.label: Turn 2 · Ask for consent to the 15:00 appointment

nodes.title: Send the consent question
nodes.detail: Ask for explicit approval of Massage with Alex at 15:00 UTC.
nodes.why: Repeating the exact service and time gives the customer a chance to catch a mistaken choice before it is booked.

nodes.title: Reserve the consent reply
nodes.detail: The sender gets the outbox ID and enforces chat ordering and rate limits.
nodes.why: Using the same sender ordering boundary keeps the consent question behind the original offer.

nodes.title: Save pending consent
nodes.detail: Publish the selected slot’s Redis state and queue the consent question.
nodes.why: Publishing pending consent with the reply gives the next turn a durable reference to the exact slot shown to the customer.

nodes.title: Ask before writing
nodes.detail: Mark the exact slot as awaiting approval and format the question.
nodes.why: Binding consent to a slot prevents a later approval from applying to a different appointment.

nodes.title: Resolve option 1
nodes.detail: Gemma finds choice 1. Laya proposes BOOK. Python matches the saved 15:00 slot.
nodes.why: The number is an index into a saved list, so matching it against that list preserves what the customer selected.

lanes.label: Turn 3 · Customer gives permission to book

nodes.title: “Yes, book it.”
nodes.detail: The approval arrives as a separate Telegram update.
nodes.why: Explicit approval in a later message separates an appointment choice from authorization to write it.

nodes.title: Save the approval update
nodes.detail: Record the approval. Its update ID will identify any booking retry.
nodes.why: The approval update ID supplies a stable key that lets the booking operation recognize a retry.

nodes.title: Wake the chat again
nodes.detail: The relay sends the chat IDs to the incoming queue.
nodes.why: Queue delivery wakes a worker while PostgreSQL continues to decide which eligible update goes next.

nodes.title: Claim the approval
nodes.detail: Lease the message and load the pointer saved after choosing option 1.
nodes.why: Per-chat ownership ensures the approval operates on the published consent state rather than racing with another turn.

nodes.title: Restore pending consent
nodes.detail: Bring the exact proposed slot into this attempt’s graph state.
nodes.why: The restored marker identifies the exact pending slot that the approval must authorize.

lanes.label: Turn 3 · Commit once and send the saved booking details

nodes.title: Send the confirmation
nodes.detail: The outbox sender delivers confirmation of the saved 15:00 appointment.
nodes.why: Reporting the persisted booking gives the customer the final appointment details after the write has succeeded.

nodes.title: Queue the final reply
nodes.detail: Save the reply and completed checkpoint pointer after the booking commits.
nodes.why: Separating the reply transaction from the booking transaction lets Telegram delivery retry without repeating the booking write.

nodes.title: Commit one booking
nodes.detail: Recheck slot and ownership. Commit the booking and retry record together.
nodes.why: Another request can take the time between offer and approval, so the transaction rechecks the slot and records the retry outcome together.

nodes.title: Execute the guarded write
nodes.detail: Recheck explicit consent and call the customer-scoped create action.
nodes.why: Checking approval again at the write boundary keeps an incorrect route from calling the booking service.

nodes.title: Verify approval and route
nodes.detail: The latest reply approves. Laya proposes BOOK for the pending 15:00 offer.
nodes.why: A fresh approval and a matching pending slot give Python concrete evidence that this specific appointment is authorized.

legend: Bold labels show the three customer turns. Dashed arrows include queue handoffs and the wait for the next Telegram message.

title: How a Telegram message moves through CAPY
subtitle: Follow the hosted RabbitMQ route from webhook intake to a leased conversation turn and a separate sender.

nodes.title: Telegram update
nodes.detail: A customer sends text, voice or a contact to the bot.
nodes.why: A private bot update carries trusted chat and sender identifiers that CAPY can tie to the customer.

nodes.title: Authenticate webhook
nodes.detail: Resolve the bot and verify the secret. Acknowledge after intake commits.
nodes.why: Verifying the bot route and secret protects the business-scoped inbox before the request is processed.

nodes.title: Save update
nodes.detail: Deduplicate the update and record due work in PostgreSQL.
nodes.why: Combining idempotent intake with a durable wake-up lets Telegram retry safely after a lost acknowledgment.

nodes.title: Relay due work
nodes.detail: Relay claims a publication and calls the broker publisher.
nodes.why: A separate relay can retry publishing while the committed inbox remains the source of the work.

nodes.title: Publish chat IDs
nodes.detail: RabbitMQ receives bot and chat IDs for the incoming queue.
nodes.why: Publishing identifiers keeps message content in the inbox and lets workers claim the current head from PostgreSQL.

nodes.title: Invoke LangGraph
nodes.detail: Run one turn in its Redis attempt thread and return the reply.
nodes.why: The invocation context keeps raw input and service objects scoped to a turn while the graph saves the conversation draft.

nodes.title: Handle the message
nodes.detail: Resolve commands and contacts or hand text and voice to the workflow.
nodes.why: Handling commands and contacts directly keeps routine channel operations out of model inference.

nodes.title: Process claimed turn
nodes.detail: Fork the prior Redis draft and resolve the customer before running the turn.
nodes.why: A single coordinator can restore the published draft, run one owned attempt, and decide which state to publish.

nodes.title: Lease chat head
nodes.detail: Claim the earliest eligible update for this bot and chat.
nodes.why: Serializing attempts for one chat preserves the meaning of short replies such as a numbered choice.

nodes.title: Consume wake-up
nodes.detail: The process role registers the chat-turn callback.
nodes.why: Broker notifications wake the worker promptly while the database enforces ordering and claim ownership.

lanes.label: Commit the reply and let the sender deliver it

nodes.title: Finish the turn
nodes.detail: Commit the checkpoint pointer and reply in PostgreSQL.
nodes.why: The reply and its checkpoint pointer become visible together, so a later answer can resume the state behind the reply.

nodes.title: Reserve the send
nodes.detail: The sender wakes by outbox ID and reserves against ordering and rate limits.
nodes.why: The reserve step coordinates reply order and rate budgets across sender processes.

nodes.title: Call Telegram
nodes.detail: Call send_reply and record the delivery outcome.
nodes.why: Recording the provider outcome lets the outbox distinguish a safe retry from a send Telegram may already have accepted.

title: Inside a LangGraph conversation turn
subtitle: Gemma extracts facts, Laya proposes the next action, and Python checks the proposed route before any write.

nodes.title: Invoke compiled graph
nodes.detail: Pass raw input and scoped actions through runtime context.
nodes.why: The runtime boundary hands raw input to the nodes that need it and keeps it out of initial checkpoint state.

nodes.title: load_context
nodes.detail: Load the business catalog and previous draft.
nodes.why: The current catalog lets the graph match real services and staff when it resumes a conversation draft.

nodes.title: understand_input
nodes.detail: Transcribe voice if present. Redact text and ask Gemma for facts.
nodes.why: Processing a complete message captures corrections and redacts recognized contact details before interpreting text.

nodes.title: merge_draft
nodes.detail: Merge current facts with the saved draft.
nodes.why: Keeping earlier facts lets a short answer such as a date fill one gap in the existing request.

nodes.title: GemmaUnderstanding
nodes.detail: Return interpreted text and structured booking facts. Voice also uses the transcription endpoint.
nodes.why: Structured facts give the workflow dates, services, and numbered choices it can validate independently.

nodes.title: LayaDecision
nodes.detail: Send message and draft to Laya and parse the proposed action.
nodes.why: A narrow routing contract limits the data passed to Laya and keeps scheduling policy in Python.

nodes.title: decide
nodes.detail: Laya receives the interpreted message and draft. Python validates the route.
nodes.why: Deterministic gates can enforce required facts, saved choices, and consent after the model proposes an action.

lanes.label: Choose an action, offer times or reply

nodes.title: prepare_action → execute
nodes.detail: Check booking ownership or the selected offer. Execute if preparation permits.
nodes.why: Preparation checks prerequisites before execution calls a service that can mutate a booking.

nodes.title: search / select
nodes.detail: Search offers slots. Select resolves a saved choice and can continue to preparation.
nodes.why: Binding a numbered reply to the original offer keeps it from selecting a different time after a new search.

nodes.title: clarify / help / lookup
nodes.detail: Ask for details, answer catalog questions or list owned bookings. Escalate shows supported options.
nodes.why: The graph can ask for missing details and answer read-only questions while leaving booking state intact.

nodes.title: BookingService
nodes.detail: Apply booking changes inside PostgreSQL transactions.
nodes.why: A transaction makes the booking change and its retry record succeed or roll back together.

nodes.title: CustomerSchedulingActions
nodes.detail: Dispatch owned operations to AvailabilityService or BookingService.
nodes.why: A customer-scoped adapter supplies trusted ownership IDs at every scheduling call.

nodes.title: persist
nodes.detail: Append the actual reply and return the turn result.
nodes.why: Saving the reply that actually went out keeps future turns grounded in what the customer saw.

nodes.title: RedisCheckpointSaver
nodes.detail: LangGraph checkpoints the attempt's state throughout execution.
nodes.why: Attempt-scoped checkpoints let later messages resume a completed draft and isolate failed work.

legend: Selected routes. The compiled graph in app/graph/builder.py shows how all reply branches converge on persist.

title: Happy path · Create a booking in three turns
subtitle: Each row starts with a new customer message. The first two turns save conversation state for the next message.

nodes.title: “Massage on Friday”
nodes.detail: Gemma extracts the service and date. Laya proposes a slot search.
nodes.why: Extracting a service and date narrows the request to concrete schedule constraints.

nodes.title: Search available slots
nodes.detail: Build the search request from the catalog and draft.
nodes.why: Constructing a typed availability request gives scheduling the same business, service, and day the conversation resolved.

nodes.title: Apply schedule rules
nodes.detail: Filter by staff hours, buffers, blocks and occupied intervals.
nodes.why: Calendar rules give both search and booking a consistent definition of a time that can be offered.

nodes.title: Return numbered offers
nodes.detail: Return a list. LangGraph checkpoints the offered slots.
nodes.why: Persisted slot IDs keep the displayed option numbers tied to the exact slots across messages.

nodes.detail: The worker forks the last completed Redis checkpoint into this attempt.
nodes.why: Restoring the previous completed turn makes a short reply meaningful without asking the customer to repeat the time.

nodes.title: Match option 1
nodes.detail: Resolve the number against the previous offer and set the pending slot.
nodes.why: Validating the index against the saved offers prevents an out-of-range or stale selection from becoming a booking request.

nodes.title: Save the consent marker
nodes.detail: Record which specific appointment is awaiting approval.
nodes.why: The saved marker tells the next turn which appointment the customer needs to approve.

nodes.title: Ask for approval
nodes.detail: Reply with the exact local time, service and professional.
nodes.why: The confirmation question lets the customer double-check the local time, service, and professional before committing.

nodes.title: “Yes”
nodes.detail: The pending offer is restored and the latest message supplies explicit consent.
nodes.why: A later, explicit approval gives the workflow customer authorization beyond the initial slot choice.

nodes.title: Verify consent and route
nodes.detail: Require clear approval, a still-offered slot and an eligible Laya BOOK proposal.
nodes.why: The exact-slot and routing checks keep ambiguous text or a changed time from reaching the creation flow.

nodes.title: Commit the booking
nodes.detail: Revalidate the slot and commit the booking and idempotency result.
nodes.why: Rechecking availability inside the write handles a competing booking that arrived after the search.

nodes.title: Return booking details
nodes.detail: Format success from the saved booking. The worker queues it for the sender.
nodes.why: Using the saved appointment for the reply makes the confirmation match what PostgreSQL committed.

legend: Arrows follow each customer turn. The booking write and Telegram reply commit in separate transactions.

title: Failure paths · What happens when a step stops
subtitle: Each row traces one condition to its handler and the resulting change in state or customer reply.

nodes.title: Bad secret, body or intake outage
nodes.detail: The webhook cannot accept the update.
nodes.why: Rejecting untrusted or invalid input protects the inbox and its downstream workers.

nodes.title: Reject the webhook
nodes.detail: Return 403 for authentication, 413 for size, 400 for invalid updates or 503 for database errors.
nodes.why: Distinct status codes tell Telegram and operators why the webhook could not accept the update.

nodes.title: No HTTP 204
nodes.detail: Telegram can retry failed intake. Accepted duplicate update IDs produce one durable receipt.
nodes.why: Acknowledgment means intake committed. An unavailable database leaves Telegram free to retry delivery.

nodes.title: Redis draft has expired
nodes.detail: The last published thread pointer no longer resolves to a checkpoint.
nodes.why: Conversation checkpoints expire to bound retained state, so an old option number may lose its original list.

nodes.title: Stop before graph execution
nodes.detail: Complete the turn with a prompt for fresh times and clear the checkpoint reference.
nodes.why: Stopping before execution avoids attaching an expired choice to the current calendar.

nodes.title: Customer can start a fresh search
nodes.detail: The expired option number is never applied to a different offer.
nodes.why: A fresh search returns a new list that the customer can select from unambiguously.

nodes.title: Redis unavailable or bot credentials unusable
nodes.detail: The worker cannot prepare the turn.
nodes.why: The worker needs working bot credentials and the published state to begin a turn safely.

nodes.title: Defer before execution
nodes.detail: Release the claim and schedule a retry.
nodes.why: Releasing the lease lets the system schedule another attempt without holding a chat during the dependency outage.

nodes.title: Retry after the delay
nodes.detail: The worker has made no customer or booking changes for this attempt.
nodes.why: Retrying a preparation failure is safe because the attempt stopped before customer or booking changes.

lanes.label: Processing · Interrupted or out of order

nodes.title: Interrupted attempt or late update
nodes.detail: The previous attempt may have committed, or the message may refer to an older offer.
nodes.why: A crash after a database write or a late update invalidates the assumptions needed to replay an ordinary turn.

nodes.title: Skip normal turn processing
nodes.detail: On interruption, clear the checkpoint reference. For a late update, retain it.
nodes.why: Clearing uncertain state or retaining the latest valid state protects the next turn from the wrong draft.

nodes.title: Ask the customer to verify or refresh
nodes.detail: After interruption, check existing appointments. For late input, request a fresh offer.
nodes.why: Checking current appointments avoids duplicating a booking whose outcome is uncertain. Refreshing offers resolves a late selection.

nodes.title: Transcription or model call fails
nodes.detail: A provider raises ProviderError before booking execution.
nodes.why: A complete interpretation is needed before CAPY can choose an action from a recording or message.

nodes.title: Return a language service reply
nodes.detail: Ask the customer to retry or send a shorter message.
nodes.why: A clear retry reply lets the customer recover when the language service cannot interpret the turn.

nodes.title: Preserve the previous checkpoint
nodes.detail: The failed attempt publishes no new draft and makes no booking change.
nodes.why: Publishing only completed state gives the next attempt the last usable draft.

nodes.title: “No,” a new time, or unclear approval
nodes.detail: The latest reply does not authorize the pending appointment.
nodes.why: Declining or changing the appointment invalidates the specific time that was offered for approval.

nodes.title: Resolve the consent guard
nodes.detail: Clear the selection on rejection or changed timing. Ask again if approval is unclear or routing cannot verify it.
nodes.why: The guard treats rejection and changed timing differently from ambiguity, which can be resolved by asking again.

nodes.title: Return a reply without creating a booking
nodes.detail: Only guarded approval for the exact slot can reach the write.
nodes.why: Leaving the booking unchanged gives the customer time to confirm the exact appointment.

lanes.label: Booking · A competing request wins the slot

nodes.title: The slot is no longer bookable
nodes.detail: Availability changes after the offer was made.
nodes.why: An offer is a snapshot of availability. A new booking may occupy it while the customer is deciding.

nodes.title: Revalidate during the transaction
nodes.detail: Reject the slot and let the graph handle the domain error.
nodes.why: Checking the current interval inside the transaction preserves the calendar when requests overlap.

nodes.title: Ask for new available times
nodes.detail: Clear the stale selection and return a fresh-search prompt.
nodes.why: Clearing the stale choice prevents a later approval from trying the unavailable slot again.

lanes.label: Delivery · Throttle, rejection or uncertain outcome

nodes.title: Telegram send fails or dispatch expires
nodes.detail: The provider may have accepted the message before a response was lost.
nodes.why: A timeout can happen after Telegram accepted a reply, so retrying blindly risks a duplicate message.

nodes.title: Classify and record the outcome
nodes.detail: Retry transient rejection such as 429. Mark permanent rejection or exhausted retries as failed.
nodes.why: A confirmed temporary rejection can be retried while permanent and uncertain outcomes need different handling.

nodes.title: Stop automatic resend if ambiguous
nodes.detail: An unknown transport outcome or expired dispatch lease becomes ambiguous.
nodes.why: An expired dispatch lease leaves delivery uncertain, which makes automatic resend unsafe.

legend: Coral marks the trigger. Links open the relevant definition in the repository.

title: Manage an existing booking
subtitle: Follow cancellation and rescheduling through the customer-scoped graph and the PostgreSQL write boundary.

nodes.title: “Cancel my appointment”
nodes.detail: A private Telegram turn resolves the trusted customer.
nodes.why: Resolving the Telegram sender first keeps a cancellation scoped to that customer's appointments.

nodes.title: Resolve the owned booking
nodes.detail: Find a selected appointment from the customer's references or ask them to choose.
nodes.why: Clarification gives the customer a chance to pick the right appointment when several match.

nodes.title: Call the scoped action
nodes.detail: Pass the business, customer and stable turn idempotency key.
nodes.why: Passing the trusted scope and stable key lets the booking service verify ownership and recognize retries.

nodes.title: Cancel and release the time
nodes.detail: Commit the canceled status and retry result. The old slot is available to offer again.
nodes.why: Keeping the canceled status and retry outcome together frees the time and preserves a stable response on replay.

nodes.title: “Move my appointment”
nodes.detail: The private Telegram turn supplies a trusted customer and a new scheduling request.
nodes.why: Starting with the trusted sender ensures the replacement search applies to an appointment that customer owns.

nodes.title: Identify booking and offer times
nodes.detail: Resolve an upcoming owned booking and search for replacement slots.
nodes.why: Identifying the original appointment provides the service and calendar context needed to find suitable replacements.

nodes.title: Match a replacement slot
nodes.detail: A later turn matches the number to the saved offer and prepares the move.
nodes.why: Matching the choice to the stored replacement offers preserves the time the customer selected.

nodes.title: Validate and commit the move
nodes.detail: Check the new interval while excluding the previous one. A failed move preserves the appointment.
nodes.why: One transaction updates the appointment only after the replacement passes validation, preserving the original on failure.

title: Evaluate a full conversation
subtitle: Follow a scenario from the CLI and YAML assertions through the real graph and its evaluation report.

lanes.label: Set up one or more scenario attempts

nodes.title: Run the scenario CLI
nodes.detail: Select the dataset, cases, providers, and repetition settings.
nodes.why: Explicit provider settings make offline regressions repeatable and enable separate live model checks.

nodes.title: Validate scenario YAML
nodes.detail: Load inputs, expected routes and writes, and final booking assertions.
nodes.why: Validating the fixture catches malformed assertions before any model or scheduling operation runs.

nodes.title: Schedule attempts
nodes.detail: Run cases and repetitions concurrently. Keep each case’s turns sequential.
nodes.why: Each attempt gets its own state, so concurrency can expose variance without mixing different conversations.

nodes.title: Set up one attempt
nodes.detail: Set up observed providers, in-memory checkpoints, and fake scheduling actions.
nodes.why: The workflow stays real while the fixture controls test dates, available slots, and booking writes.

lanes.label: Run the workflow and collect results

nodes.title: Review the HTML report
nodes.detail: Inspect attempts, transcripts, failures, timing, and coverage.
nodes.why: Per-case evidence shows which turn failed and gives a maintainer a concrete place to investigate.

nodes.title: Build the run receipt
nodes.detail: Record the revision, manifests, provider settings, and attempt results.
nodes.why: A saved receipt ties a score to its exact inputs and allows a later result to be compared or replayed.

nodes.title: Check writes and outcomes
nodes.detail: Compare turn and final assertions. The optional judge reviews reply quality.
nodes.why: Deterministic checks catch permission and write failures even when the response sounds plausible.

nodes.title: Run each graph turn
nodes.detail: Send each fixture message through the workflow and capture provider and reply evidence.
nodes.why: Running the same graph exposes problems that only appear when interpretation, routing, and saved state interact.

title: Verify CAPY across test layers
subtitle: See what CI exercises and open representative tests for routing, evaluation, and real scheduling services.

nodes.title: Run the CI checks
nodes.detail: Start PostgreSQL, Redis, and RabbitMQ. Run pytest, the offline eval corpus, and Compose checks.
nodes.why: A controlled environment makes the required services available and catches changes before they land.

nodes.title: Unit and API tests
nodes.detail: Use fixtures and fakes to test graph, adapters, models, and readiness behavior.
nodes.why: Small and deterministic checks make policy and request-contract failures easy to localize.

nodes.title: Evaluation tests
nodes.detail: Exercise task scoring and run controlled multi-turn scenarios.
nodes.why: These checks catch implicit changes to datasets, scoring, or model configuration.

nodes.title: Integration tests
nodes.detail: Apply migrations and use disposable services for real scheduling, state, and broker checks.
nodes.why: Locks, recovery, and database constraints need exercise against compatible services.

nodes.title: Guard pending consent
nodes.detail: Assert that an incorrect cancel proposal cannot mutate the existing booking.
nodes.why: A model routing mistake should never become a booking change while another appointment is awaiting consent.

nodes.title: Verify the golden case
nodes.detail: Inspect Gemma and Laya evidence and require a separate approval before the first write.
nodes.why: The test ties model outputs to the observable booking effect of each turn.

nodes.title: Run a booking lifecycle
nodes.detail: Book, move, and cancel an appointment through the real scheduling services.
nodes.why: The lifecycle verifies that the conversation’s decisions make the intended PostgreSQL changes over multiple turns.

legend: Arrows connect CI to test layers and each layer to a representative source test.
